slides.title: Three weeks of debate, zero decisions
slides.tldr: Not deciding has a price: features stall, the loudest voice wins, and the reasoning gets lost.

blocks.body: Monday stand-up. Sarah says, "Let's use RabbitMQ for the queue." Jake says, "We already have Redis. Why add something new?" Three weeks later, nobody has said anything wrong, and nobody has decided anything either. The feature has been stuck the whole time.

blocks.title: What not deciding costs
items: The feature stays stuck and the business earns later.
Whoever speaks loudest wins, not whoever has the better reasoning.
Everyone digs in on their favorite, and nobody asks "why" any more.

blocks.caption: A debating meeting vs a deciding meeting

columns.title: Debating meeting
items: Starts with "I feel that…"
No agreed criteria
Ends with "let's see later"
columns.tip: Everyone fights for their own pick, and nobody has agreed on what the options will be judged by.

columns.title: Deciding meeting
items: Criteria and weights set first
Options side by side on one page
One decision-maker, with a date
columns.tip: The criteria are agreed first, then the options are measured, so everyone looks at the same scale.

blocks.body: Not deciding is also a decision. It's just one nobody chose on purpose.

aside.title: The notification queue
aside.body: At one startup, the argument over which queue to use ran for a month. Then the CTO wrote four criteria on a single page and made the call within an hour. For the next three months, nobody questioned it.
This segment shows how to turn an argument into criteria, reach a decision, and recover quickly when the decision turns out wrong.

check.q: Nobody is wrong, yet three weeks went by without a decision. What is the core gap?
check.a: The criteria were never agreed in advance, and nobody owned the decision. So the debate was only a contest of preferences.

slides.title: All the good things never come together
slides.tldr: Every option gives you something and costs you something. The question is not "which is best?" but "which quality do we need most?"

blocks.title: Going home for Thanksgiving
blocks.body: Before Thanksgiving, you can head home by bus, train or ferry. The bus ticket is easy to get, but you may sit in a traffic jam. The train arrives on time, but its tickets are hard to find. Which one is "best" depends on whether time, cost or comfort matters most to you.

blocks.caption: The Thanksgiving trip: three options, four criteria

rows.tip: The bus wins on this criterion. But an easy ticket does not mean a good journey.
For someone who must be home by a fixed time, this is the train's biggest advantage.
If keeping costs down is the goal, the train comes out ahead.
None of them wins on every criterion. That is what a trade-off is.

blocks.body: There is no best option. There is only the option that best fits your criteria.

items: Write down the criteria before you look at the options. Do it the other way around and you'll be tempted to build criteria that favor your pick.
Keep at least two options. "Do nothing" counts as one.

check.q: Bus, train or ferry: why is there no single answer to "which is best?"
check.a: Because none of them wins on every criterion. The answer depends on whether time, cost or comfort matters most to you.

slides.title: Decision matrix: weighing options on one page
slides.tldr: Write the criteria, give each a weight, score each option, multiply and add. Then change the weights to see whether the result holds.

blocks.body: Let's put Sarah and Jake's debate on one page. There are three options for the Symfony Messenger transport. Weights run from 1 to 5, and so do the scores. Each total below is the sum of score times weight.

blocks.code:
Question: Which Messenger transport?   Decider: Sarah   Date: 12 December

Criterion (weight)          Doctrine   Redis   RabbitMQ
----------------------------------------------
Easy to operate (3)            5         4        2
Messages never lost (3)        4         3        5
Team experience (2)            4         4        2
Future throughput (2)          2         4        5
----------------------------------------------
Total                         39        37       35

Sensitivity: raise the weight of "future throughput" from 2 to 5 and
Doctrine 45, Redis 49, RabbitMQ 50 - the winner changes.

Decision: Doctrine transport. We handle fewer than 2,000 messages a day.
Revisit if: volume passes 100,000 a day, or a message is ever lost.

marks.tip: The weights are fixed before any scoring. Otherwise you'll be tempted to change them to help your favorite win.
When the totals are close, the decision hangs on the weights. Change them and see whether the result holds.
The winner changed, so the real discussion is about weights: how much do we care about growth we may never reach?
Both the reason and the trigger for rethinking are written down, so someone asking in six months gets an answer.

blocks.caption: Same options, different weights, different winner

items.label: Doctrine (original)
items.tip: Wins under the first weights: easy operation and team experience count for a lot here.

items.label: Redis (original)
items.tip: Only 2 points behind, which means close to a tie.

items.label: RabbitMQ (original)
items.tip: Behind on operation and experience, so third.

items.label: Doctrine (throughput 5)
items.tip: Same scores, new weight: Doctrine gains only a little, because it scores low on throughput.

items.label: RabbitMQ (throughput 5)
items.tip: Give future throughput more weight and RabbitMQ wins.

blocks.body: A matrix doesn't find the truth. It only shows which assumptions each decision rests on.

items: Numbers are not science. They are estimates made by judgment, so write the reasoning next to them.
Skip the matrix for a choice you can undo in a day. Pick one, ship it and learn.
With more than 10 criteria, the two or three that really matter get lost.

aside.body: Criteria first, then weights, then scores. Finally, change the weights and see whether the result holds.

check.q: Two options have nearly equal totals in a matrix. What is the next step?
check.a: Change the weights and see whether the winner changes. If it does, discuss the weights, because that is where the real disagreement is.

slides.title: Deciding without all the facts: which way does the door swing?
slides.tldr: Make reversible decisions fast and irreversible ones slowly. Waiting for every fact means the chance is gone.

blocks.body: Thanksgiving train tickets go on sale at 8 a.m. There is no way to know in advance how big the crowd in the online queue will be. If you wait, the tickets sell out, so you have to buy on a guess. In software, 100% of the facts never arrive either. The real question is whether you can undo the decision if it turns out wrong.

blocks.caption: Two kinds of doors, two kinds of speed

columns.title: Reversible (decide fast)
items: New behavior behind a feature flag
Swapping a library
A one-week experiment (spike)
columns.tip: A mistake here costs little. It's better to move fast and learn.

columns.title: Irreversible (decide slowly)
items: Public API responses
The data model, ID types
Getting locked into a database or cloud
columns.tip: A mistake here takes months to fix. So take time to think, and ask others.

blocks.title: Five rules for deciding under uncertainty
items: First, decide which way the door swings.
For reversible decisions, go ahead once you have about 70% of the facts.
For irreversible ones, write an RFC and let two or three people review it before you commit.
Write down the assumptions you are making.
Decide in advance what sign will make you rethink.

aside.title: The ID type
aside.body: A team stored order IDs as plain counting numbers (1, 2, 3...) because "we need to move now". Two years later, those IDs had spread through their partners' systems. Changing them took six months. One afternoon of thought at the start, and a random ID like a UUID, would have cost almost nothing. A door that doesn't swing back should never have been walked through in a hurry.

items.meaning: A switch in configuration that turns a feature on or off without a new deploy.
A short, throwaway experiment whose only job is to teach you something.

items.label: Can you walk back through the door?

check.q: Which decision deserves more time: a new button behind a feature flag, or changing a public API response?
check.a: The public API response. Changing it breaks mobile apps and partners, and you can't take it back. The button can be switched off with the flag in a minute.

slides.title: The risk list: impact × likelihood
slides.tldr: You can't handle every risk. Score each one's likelihood and impact from 1 to 5, multiply, and tackle the biggest first.

blocks.body: A pharmacy owner doesn't stock every medicine equally. A medicine that is rarely needed but fatal to be without comes first. Risks work the same way: pick the big ones by combining likelihood and impact. Write them down in a risk register.

blocks.code:
# Risk                         Likelihood  Impact  Score  Action               Owner
R1 Payment gateway down 2 hrs       3         5      15   circuit breaker +    Jake
                                                          "try again later" msg
R2 Migration locks the table        3         4      12   run on a quiet night, Sarah
                                                          try on staging first
R3 Only expert is on leave          4         2       8   write a runbook      Ryan
R4 Complaints about login color    5         1       5   do nothing           -

Score = likelihood × impact (1-5 × 1-5)
Rule: 12 or more -> work on it this sprint. 6-11 -> backlog, with a date.
      5 or less -> accept it knowingly.

marks.tip: The highest score, so it comes first. The likelihood is only medium, but the impact is enormous.
Likelihood is high but impact is small, so the score is low. A runbook is a cheap fix here.
"Do nothing" is also a decision. Written down, it gives you an answer when someone asks later.
With the rules agreed in advance, there is less arguing about which work to pick by score.

blocks.caption: Risk scores (likelihood × impact), maximum 25

items.label: R1 gateway down
items.tip: The biggest risk: if payments fail, revenue stops.

items.label: R2 migration lock
items.tip: By the rule, this is also work for this sprint.

items.label: R3 expert on leave
items.tip: Important, but there is a cheap fix: a runbook.

items.label: R4 login color
items.tip: A small risk. Accepting it is reasonable.

items: Listing only what frightens you. What is uncomfortable but real gets left out.
Scores are rough guesses. Don't spend an hour arguing whether something is a 3 or a 4.
Writing it once and forgetting it. Review the register every month.

aside.body: Likelihood × impact = priority. Every risk gets one owner and one action.

items.meaning: A switch that stops calling a broken service for a while, so one failure doesn't drag everything else down.
A step-by-step page, "if X breaks, do this", so anyone on the team can fix it, not just the expert.

check.q: R3 has a likelihood of 4, so why is its score low, and what was done about it?
check.a: Its impact is only 2, so 4×2 = 8. A cheap action was taken instead of spending a lot: writing a runbook.

slides.title: When you spot a mistake: the sooner you admit it, the cheaper it is
slides.tldr: Carrying on down the wrong path because you've already spent a lot is the sunk cost trap. Say it fast, reverse, and write down the lesson.

blocks.body: Jake has spent three months building his own search module. Now it turns out a standard Symfony approach does the same job. He thinks, "I've worked so hard. How can I throw it away?" That thought is the sunk cost fallacy: what's already spent won't come back, so it has no place in the calculation of the future.

blocks.caption: Four steps after you spot a mistake

steps.title: 1. Say it plainly
steps.body: Tell the team: "I found a mistake, and it was my decision."
steps.tip: Saying it first builds trust. If someone else finds it, it looks like it was being hidden.

steps.title: 2. Stop the damage
steps.body: Spend nothing more yet. First find a way back.
steps.tip: Stop the bleeding before repairing: turn off the feature flag, roll back, or pause the work.

steps.title: 3. Weigh what remains
steps.body: Compare only what it costs from now: to finish vs to replace.
steps.tip: The three months already spent are equal on both sides, so leave them out of the calculation.

steps.title: 4. Write the lesson
steps.body: A blameless postmortem: what happened, why, and what will change.
steps.tip: Look for the gap in the process, not someone to blame. Otherwise next time everyone will hide mistakes.

blocks.code:
Already spent: 12 weeks. Gone on both paths, so leave it out of the sum.

Path A, finish our own search module:      4 more weeks, and we maintain it for good
Path B, switch to the standard Symfony way: 1 week, and it is maintained for us

Cheaper from today: B (1 week vs 4). Switch, and write down why.
Flip the numbers (A = 1 week, B = 4) and the answer flips: finish it.

marks.tip: The 12 weeks are identical whether you carry on or stop, so they cannot tip the choice.
Only the future cost of each path goes in the comparison.
The rule is the comparison, not "always throw it away". Sometimes finishing is cheaper.

blocks.body: Admitting a mistake is cheapest today. Every day it gets dearer.

aside.title: Who spoke first
aside.body: At one team, a bad migration wiped some order data. The junior developer reported it himself within ten minutes. By the next few hours everything was restored from backup. Word got around the next day. Had it been hidden, the damage could have run on for a week.

items: Thank a junior who admits a mistake instead of punishing them. Otherwise nobody will report the next one.
Learn to say, "I misjudged it, and now I know." It makes you more credible as a leader.

check.q: "I've worked on it for three months, so let's carry on." What is wrong with this reasoning?
check.a: The time already spent won't come back either way. The decision should rest on the remaining cost and the future benefit.

slides.title: One slide, four people, four kinds of confusion
slides.tldr: A sound design explained in the wrong language lands with no one. Each listener asks a different question, so each needs a different answer.

blocks.body: Sarah has built a good design: after payment, the remaining work goes onto a queue. She takes the same slide to four people. The engineer asks how retries will work, and she says "event-driven." Finance asks what it costs, and she says "scalable." Nobody is satisfied, and the project stalls.

blocks.caption: One slide went to four people, and none got an answer

nodes.label: Sarah's slide
nodes.tip: A single slide full of technology words. It answers nobody's question.

nodes.label: Engineer
nodes.tip: Wanted the failure path and the retries. Got one buzzword.

nodes.label: Product
nodes.tip: Wanted to know how the user experience will change.

nodes.label: Auditor
nodes.tip: Wanted evidence that the rules are being followed.

edges.label: The engineer asked how retries work and heard "event-driven"
Product asked what changes for users and got no answer
Finance asked about cost and heard "scalable"
The auditor asked for proof and the slide had nothing

blocks.title: What went wrong
items: The same slide was shown to four different audiences.
Each listener came with a different question, and none got an answer.
It had words like "event-driven" and "scalable", but no numbers and no consequences.

blocks.title: One medicine, at the pharmacy
blocks.body: Tell a patient "twice a day, after meals." Tell the doctor the dose and the gap between doses. Tell the pharmacist the batch and the expiry date. It's the same medicine and the same facts, but the words change with the listener.
One design, but the way you explain it changes with the listener.

aside.title: Finance's three questions
aside.body: An engineer asking for a new cloud budget explained CPU and autoscaling. The CFO asked only three questions: what will it cost, what do we get, and what happens if we don't do it? Answering those three in one line would have won approval in 10 minutes.
This segment teaches you to explain one design to four audiences, write a one-page design doc, and run a review that doesn't turn into a courtroom.

check.q: Why did Sarah's slide fail, even though the design was right?
check.a: Every listener had a different question, but all got the same answer. "Event-driven" and "scalable" answer nobody's question.

slides.title: Four audiences, four questions
slides.tldr: Engineers ask how. Product asks what changes for users. Finance asks what it costs. Regulators ask for proof.

blocks.body: Each audience keeps asking one question, so find out what it is before you speak. Answer it in their language and they'll trust the rest. The technical detail you care about is no use to them. The table below gives each audience's core question and what to hand them.

blocks.caption: Four audiences: what they ask, what you give

cells: How will it work, and how will it break?
rows.tip: Engineers want depth. Show where it can break first; that is what they will look for anyway.

cells: What will users get, and when?
rows.tip: To product, "queue" means nothing; "the email arrives up to 2 minutes late" means something.

cells: How much money, what return, what if not?
Cost, gain or loss avoided, timeline
rows.tip: Without numbers, finance can't decide. Even if it's an estimate, give a range.

cells: What proves we follow the rules?
Controls, logs, where the data lives
rows.tip: To an auditor, "we do it properly" isn't enough. Show a record of who did what, and when.

blocks.body: Find out what question the listener came with, then open your mouth.

items: Before the meeting, ask the listener: "What matters most to you in this decision?"
Don't make four slide decks. Write four summaries of the same design, one paragraph each.

aside.body: Engineer: how. Product: what changes. Finance: how much. Auditor: what proof.

check.q: Instead of explaining "autoscaling" to finance, what is better to say?
check.a: The approximate monthly cost, the benefit you get, and the loss if you don't do it. Numbers and consequences, not technology.

slides.title: One design, four languages
slides.tldr: The design: after payment, the rest of the work goes on a queue. Four summaries, each written as an answer to that audience's question.

blocks.body: Here is the design: after the customer pays, the email, invoice and accounting work moves onto a queue instead of running inside the request. Below, the same design is written for four audiences. The numbers are examples; put in your own facts.

blocks.code:
[Engineer]
POST /checkout writes only the payment and order status, plus an outbox row (a
to-do note) in the same transaction. A Messenger worker takes the rest; handlers
are idempotent (safe to run twice), retry 3 times, then go to the failed queue.
Target: p95 (the slowest 1 checkout in 20) from 4 s to under 1 s.

[Product]
Checkout will finish in 1 second instead of 4. "Order confirmed" shows
immediately; the email can arrive up to 2 minutes late. The trade-off: the
email is no longer instant. Goal: fewer abandoned carts.

[Finance]
Extra cost: 1 worker, about $150 a month (example). Expected gain: a
share of the orders lost to slow checkout comes back. If we don't do it: losses
grow in the holiday sales season. Trial launch in 2 weeks.

[Regulator / auditor]
We don't store card data; the payment provider does. Every payment and each
follow-up event goes into an audit log with a date, and cannot be altered. Log
retention: as the rules require (example: 5 years).

marks.tip: For the engineer: the structure and the failure path, meaning where it writes and what happens when it breaks.
For product: the user experience, and a clear statement of what is being given up.
For finance: cost, gain and the price of not doing it, all with numbers.
For the auditor: the evidence, meaning where the data lives and why it can't be altered.

blocks.body: Every summary starts from the listener's question, not from the technology.

items: Showing finance an estimate as if it were certain. Give a range: "6,000 to 10,000".
Hiding the trade-off from product. If you don't say "the email will be late", it comes back later as a surprise.

check.q: What is the main difference in explaining the same queue design to finance and to the auditor?
check.a: Give finance the cost, the gain and the price of doing nothing. Give the auditor proof: where each piece of data lives, and who did what, when.

slides.title: Design doc / RFC: a decision on one page
slides.tldr: A good RFC holds the problem, the options, the proposal, the risks and the ask, all in one place, so people can read it and respond.

blocks.body: A decision made out loud is forgotten later. An RFC (Request for Comments) is a page or two of writing that gives everyone a chance to respond. Copy the structure below. Clear writing is worth more than long writing.

blocks.code:
# RFC-0012: Move post-order work onto a queue
Author: Sarah   Status: Draft   Decider: Ryan   Comments due: 20 December

## 1. Problem (2-3 lines)
Checkout takes 4 seconds; customers leave when it takes more than 3.

## 2. Goals and non-goals
Goal: p95 under 1 second. Non-goal: a new email design.

## 3. Options (at least two, including "do nothing")
A. Do nothing  B. Fix the queries  C. Move work to a queue

## 4. Proposal and why
C. With B, the delay only drops to 1.5 seconds and misses the goal.

## 5. Risks and the way back
Delayed emails. A switch (a feature flag) lets us return to the old path.

## 6. What I'm asking for
Engineering and product feedback by 20 December; then Ryan decides.

marks.tip: The decider and the deadline go at the top. Otherwise an RFC stays open forever.
The problem comes first. However good the solution, nobody can judge it without understanding the problem.
Saying what you are not doing keeps the feedback on the main question and cuts side arguments.
Without options, no one can tell whether anything else was considered. "Do nothing" is always an option.
With the risks and the way back written down, the decision becomes easier to make.

blocks.caption: An RFC's journey: from writing to a decision

steps.title: 1. Write
steps.body: Problem, options, proposal, in 1-2 pages.
steps.tip: If it's long, nobody reads it. Past 2 pages, split it.

steps.title: 2. Collect feedback
steps.body: Set a deadline, and tell two or three people by name.
steps.tip: Telling everyone means telling no one. Naming people gets you feedback.

steps.title: 3. Decide
steps.body: When time is up, the decider writes the decision, with reasons.
steps.tip: When the discussion ends, one person decides, even if not everyone agrees.

steps.title: 4. Keep it
steps.body: Set the status to Accepted and store it in the repo.
steps.tip: Six months on, a new member asks "why?"; this is the answer.

items: Write the risks of your own proposal first; an RFC whose author names its weaknesses is the one people trust more.
For smaller decisions, use an ADR (Architecture Decision Record): context, decision, consequences, in three paragraphs.

check.q: Why does the "Options" section of an RFC include "do nothing"?
check.a: It is always a real option. Without it, the reader can't tell whether the work is really worth its price.

slides.title: Run a review, not a trial
slides.tldr: A review judges the design, not the person. With the right rules, authors don't hide weaknesses; they mention them up front.

blocks.body: Ryan is presenting his design in a review, and someone asks, "How did you even come up with this?" He gets defensive. Next time, he'll come to the review without mentioning the weak spots. If a review is a courtroom, the author's only goal is not to get caught.

blocks.caption: A courtroom review vs a collaborative review

columns.title: Courtroom
items: "Why didn't you think of this?"
The reviewer hunts for fault
Ends without a decision or next steps
columns.tip: The questions are aimed at the person. The author gets scared and hides information.

columns.title: Collaboration
items: "What happens if this part breaks?"
The reviewer looks for risks and offers alternatives
Ends with a decision and an action list
columns.tip: The questions are aimed at the design. The author states the weaknesses first.

blocks.code:
0-5    Author: the problem and proposal, and the part they doubt most
5-15   Reviewers: questions (questions first, opinions later)
15-25  Discussion: risks and alternatives; the author takes notes, doesn't argue
25-30  Decision: Accept / Accept with changes / Review again; action list

marks.tip: When the author names the doubtful part, the review's attention goes there.
Asking first cuts misunderstandings; opinions come afterwards.
Choosing one of three defined outcomes keeps the review from dangling.

blocks.body: Question the design, not the designer.

aside.title: The hidden weakness
aside.body: On one team, the author knew his migration had a risk but didn't mention it in the review, because last time he'd taken harsh criticism. The risk was caught in production. In a safe review culture, he would have said it up front.

items: Starting a comment with "Tell me if I've misunderstood" makes the question easier to take.
At the end of the review, ask one person to send out the action list.

check.q: Instead of "How did you even come up with this?", what is better to say in a review?
check.a: A question about the design, such as "What happens if this part breaks?" or "Did you look at this alternative?" The question points at the design, not the person.

slides.title: The design is right, but nobody is listening
slides.tldr: You can build influence without a title. Being right isn't enough; people listen to the person they trust.

blocks.body: Sarah realizes that direct database queries to the order service are scattered everywhere and will break soon. She posts in Slack, "This needs fixing." Nobody replies. Six months later, exactly that breaks, and everyone says, "You should have told us!" She did. But she never brought anyone along.

blocks.title: The captain of the neighborhood soccer team
blocks.body: Nobody appointed the captain of the neighborhood team. Yet everyone listens to her, because she plays alongside them, takes the risks first, and explains what needs to happen on the field. Influence doesn't come from a title. It comes from trust.

blocks.caption: The power of position vs the power of influence

columns.title: Power of position
items: "The manager said so, do it"
Change the title and the power goes
No real buy-in inside
columns.tip: You can give orders, but people won't do the work wholeheartedly.

columns.title: Power of influence
items: "What they say is usually right"
Everyone feels the decision is theirs
Buy-in comes from within
columns.tip: Influence built on trust works even without a title.

blocks.body: Being right is one job. Bringing people with you is another.

aside.body: This segment teaches you to bring people along without a title, to grow newer colleagues, and to know when to stop arguing and decide.
Trust first, argument second. We listen closely to the people we trust.

check.q: Why did Sarah's warning go nowhere, even though she was right?
check.a: She only said it and never brought anyone along. Influence is built on trust, numbers and small proofs, not just on saying the right thing.

slides.title: Influence without a title: four steps
slides.tldr: Listen first, then show evidence, run a small pilot and find an ally. Persuade with proof, not pressure.

blocks.body: This time Sarah goes about it differently. She first goes to people on the team and asks what problems they have. Then she brings real evidence. These four steps turn an idea into a team decision, with no title required.

blocks.caption: Four steps to turn an idea into a team decision

steps.title: 1. Listen first
steps.body: Ask each person about their problems, and frame the problem in their words.
steps.tip: Understand their problem before you pitch your solution. People want to hear a solution to their own problem.

steps.title: 2. Show numbers
steps.body: How often it broke, how many hours it cost, what could happen next month.
steps.tip: "This needs fixing" is an opinion. "It cost us 14 hours in the last three months" is a fact.

steps.title: 3. Run a small pilot
steps.body: Try the new approach in one module and show the result.
steps.tip: It's easier to get permission for a small trial than for a big change, and you get proof.

steps.title: 4. Find an ally
steps.body: Win over one respected colleague first.
steps.tip: When a second person says the same thing in the meeting, trust doubles.

blocks.code:
Problem:   Order queries are spread over 12 places; a schema change breaks all.
Evidence:  3 hotfixes for this in the last 3 months, 14 hours in total.
Proposal:  Move all queries into one OrderRepository, starting with reports.
Cost:      2 days, I'll do it; nobody else's work is blocked.
Way back:  If it doesn't work out, reverting one PR restores the old state.
Ask:       In a week, look at the result and decide together.

marks.tip: Evidence in numbers. Facts, not opinions.
The cost is small and in your own hands, so there are fewer reasons to say no.
Showing a way back lowers the risk and makes it easier to say yes.

blocks.body: Don't ask permission for a big change. Ask for a small trial, and bring the proof.

items: Presenting the idea for the first time in a meeting. Talk to people one by one first and learn where they stand.
Winning by proving someone wrong. They'll accept it, but they won't cooperate.
Using a pilot to stall. If the problem is urgent or dangerous, such as a security hole, skip the campaign and escalate now.

items.label: Explaining the cost of tech debt

check.q: Why is running a small pilot smarter than asking permission for a big refactor?
check.a: A small pilot carries little risk, so permission comes easily. And once you have the result, you have evidence for the bigger decision.

slides.title: Mentoring: questions, not answers
slides.tldr: A good mentor doesn't pour out answers. They ask questions that teach thinking, meet regularly and share stories of their own mistakes.

blocks.body: Junior developer Jake comes over and says, "This query is slow. What should I do?" If the senior just tells him the answer, he'll fix it today and be back next time. If the senior asks, "What does EXPLAIN, the command that shows how the database runs a query, tell you?", he'll dig around on his own and manage alone next time.

blocks.caption: Giving the answer vs asking a question

columns.title: Direct answer
items: "Add an index."
The problem goes away today
Another question next time
columns.tip: Today's problem is solved, but nothing is learned. The mentor becomes a bottleneck.

columns.title: Asking questions
items: "What do you see in EXPLAIN?"
He finds the cause himself
Next time he solves it alone
columns.tip: Slower, but Jake does the thinking. That habit is an asset for life.

blocks.file: A question ladder for one slow query
blocks.code:
Jake:   "This query is slow."
Senior:  "How slow, and how do you know?"          -> learns to measure
Jake:   "About 4 seconds."
Senior:  "What is the biggest step in EXPLAIN?"    -> learns to read the plan
Jake:   "It reads every row of the orders table."
Senior:  "How could it find the rows without reading all?"   -> the index is his idea
Jake:   "An index on customer_id?"

marks.tip: First question: measure. "Slow" is a feeling; 4 seconds is a fact.
Second: read the evidence. He learns to open EXPLAIN himself.
Third: let him name the fix. Three questions take longer than one sentence, but next time he asks himself all three.

blocks.code:
1. What went well this week?            (5 min, morale)
2. Where are you stuck?                 (10 min; questions, not solutions)
3. One skill to grow this month         (5 min; a specific goal)
4. What do you need from me?            (5 min)
5. A mistake or lesson of mine          (5 min; it opens people up)

marks.tip: Questions instead of solutions: "What have you tried? What do you think the cause is?"
Mentoring runs on small goals: this month, learn to read one EXPLAIN.
Telling your own mistake story shows a junior that mistakes are normal, not shameful.

blocks.body: Don't hand a junior a fish. Give them a net.

items: Make code review a chance to teach: write comments that explain "why".
Sometimes a direct answer is right: if production is down, fix it first, then teach.

use: The junior has tried, and the problem is not new to them
There is time, and the problem isn't urgent
avoid: Production is down and you're in a hurry
They are brand new and have no base to ask questions from

check.q: When is a direct answer right, and when should you ask questions?
check.a: In an emergency, or on a topic that is completely new to them, answer directly. When there is time and the junior has tried something, ask questions and make them think.

slides.title: Consensus doesn't mean everyone agrees
slides.tldr: Consensus means "I may not fully agree, but I can live with this." No serious objection is enough; full agreement isn't required.

blocks.body: At a homeowners' association meeting, not every neighbor agrees on everything. The chair asks, "Does anyone have an objection they can't live with?" If nobody does, the decision stands. A team decision works the same way: the goal isn't 100% support, it's no serious objection.

blocks.caption: Three levels of agreement, person by person

rows.tip: Fully on board. These people are the energy that carries the work forward.

cells: I'd do it differently, but I won't block it
rows.tip: The common and healthy state. Not everyone gets their first choice.

cells: This causes me a serious problem
rows.tip: This is the objection that matters; it may carry a risk or a fact the others don't know.

blocks.title: The path to agreement
items: Before the meeting, talk one by one with the main objectors about the proposal (pre-wire).
In the meeting, ask: "Does anyone have a serious objection?" Look for objections, not a head count.
If there is an objection, write down its reason and look for a fix or an alternative.

blocks.body: Don't wait for everyone to agree. Ask whether anyone has a serious objection.

aside.title: Silent agreement
aside.body: In one meeting, everyone stayed quiet and the chair assumed everyone agreed. Later it turned out two people had serious objections but hadn't voiced them in front of the seniors. Each person's view should have been collected separately first.

items: Taking silence for agreement. Ask each person by name.
When a senior speaks first, the rest follow. Let the juniors speak first.
Chasing consensus on every decision. It costs time; for small, reversible choices let the owner decide (next slide).

check.q: Sarah said "I can live with it." What does that mean, and what does the team do?
check.a: She would have done it differently but won't block it. The team can note her concern and move ahead.

slides.title: When to stop arguing: disagree and commit
slides.tldr: Set a time limit, then one person decides and everyone moves ahead wholeheartedly. Only for decisions you can undo; never for safety, security or ethics.

blocks.body: An argument can run forever. A good team knows when to end it. The rule: one person is the decider, the discussion has a time limit, and at the end a decision is made. Whoever disagrees writes down their view, then works wholeheartedly for the decision.

blocks.caption: Four steps from argument to decision

steps.title: 1. Set a time limit
steps.body: Fix the end of the discussion (say, Thursday).
steps.tip: Without a deadline, arguments don't end. The cost of extra debate is higher than the value of the decision.

steps.title: 2. One decider
steps.body: Name them up front: whoever carries the most responsibility.
steps.tip: Whoever is accountable decides. Not a committee.

steps.title: 3. Write down dissent
steps.body: Record the other view and its reasons.
steps.tip: When a dissenting view is written down, the person feels heard.

steps.title: 4. Commit fully
steps.body: No working around the decision by the back door.
steps.tip: Commit doesn't mean obeying reluctantly. It means trying to make the decision succeed.

blocks.code:
Date: 14 December    Decider: Ryan
Question: Should notifications be a separate service?
Decision: No, for now a module inside the main app.
Reason: The team is 4 people; a separate service's operating cost is too much now.
Dissent: Sarah - a separate service would make scaling easier later.
Reversible: Yes. Extracting the module later costs about 2 weeks.
Revisit: When the team reaches 8, or notifications pass 1,000,000 a day.

marks.tip: The decider's name and the date: who, and when.
With her dissent recorded, Sarah feels heard, and if she turns out right, everyone will know.
The test for using this method at all. If this line said "No, it can't be undone", we would not simply commit and move on.
It says when to rethink. 1,000,000 a day is about 12 every second, so the trigger is real growth.

blocks.title: When not to "disagree and commit"
items: The decision is hard to undo: deleting data, or signing a contract with no exit. Slow down and ask for evidence first.
The objection is about safety, security, law or ethics, such as logging full card numbers to debug faster. That is not a dissent to file away; stop it and escalate.
New facts arrived after the decision. Bring them to the decider and ask for a rethink.

blocks.body: You can follow a decision you disagree with, but a team drowns in argument without one.

use: The decision is reversible and the cost of arguing is high
Both options are about equally good
avoid: There is a serious security or legal risk; you can't stay silent
New facts have arrived since the decision; think again

aside.body: Open in the discussion, one voice in the decision, everyone together in the work.

check.q: After the decision is made, what should Sarah do if she still disagrees?
check.a: Her dissent is already on record, so she works wholeheartedly for the decision. If new facts arrive, she can raise the question again.

slides.title: A flawless app, and Black Friday has come and gone
slides.tldr: Design without understanding the business goal solves the wrong problem, however good the code. An engineer's job is to turn goals into constraints.

blocks.body: Marketing wanted to launch a "Black Friday offer" two weeks before Black Friday. Jake's team said it would take two months, because they wanted to build everything "properly". The offer went live a week after Black Friday. The code was flawless, but the selling season was over.

blocks.title: The bakery before Thanksgiving
blocks.body: Before Thanksgiving, a baker knows that however beautiful the pie, one that doesn't reach the customer before Thanksgiving morning means nothing to them. So she first works out what must be ready by tomorrow and what can wait two more days.

blocks.caption: The same two months, seen two ways

columns.title: Seeing only the technology
items: "I'll release when it's all done properly"
The deadline is the business's, and was forgotten
Season over, customers at another store
columns.tip: The engineer's care for good code is right, but the business deadline was dropped.

columns.title: Understanding the business goal
items: "What must be there before Black Friday?"
Core in 2 weeks, the rest later
Sales in season, polish afterwards
columns.tip: It first found out what the offer cannot live without, and left the rest for later.

blocks.body: Without knowing the business goal, even the best code solves the wrong problem.

aside.body: This segment teaches you to turn business goals into design constraints, work out ROI, balance time against quality, and treat legal rules as design input.
Ask: "What does the business want, and what does it lose if it doesn't get it?"

check.q: Why was Jake's team's flawless app no use to the business?
check.a: The Black Friday season was the offer's whole value. The deadline was a business constraint, and by holding out for quality the team missed the chance.

slides.title: From business goals to design constraints
slides.tldr: Turn each business goal into a measurable quality attribute, and only then choose the design.

blocks.body: "Customers must never lose money" is business talk. In engineering terms, it means correctness and an audit trail you can check later. "Lots of customers on Black Friday" means scalability, coping when many arrive at once. This translation is the architect's job. Without it, a design stands on guesswork.

blocks.caption: From a business goal to a design decision

rows.tip: Get the numbers: how many times more, and for how long. You can't design from "a lot".
With money, correctness beats speed. There is no room to compromise here.

cells: A simple monolith, buy rather than build
rows.tip: A deadline is the hardest constraint on a design; a complex architecture is a burden here.
The law can't be changed. It is a constraint to assume before design starts.

blocks.code:
Goal:         Handle 10x orders in Black Friday week without losing a single order
Measure:      peak 500 orders/min; p95 checkout < 1 second; lost orders = 0
Assumption:   last year's peak was 50 orders/min (from analytics); no new hires in 3 months
Constraint:   small team -> no new services; add a queue to the current monolith
Will give up: admin reports will stay slow
Won't give up: accuracy of money and orders

marks.tip: Numbers make "a lot" measurable: 500 orders a minute is about 8 every second, like 8 people reaching a coffee shop counter each second. p95 means 95 of every 100 customers finish checkout in under 1 second.
Write the assumptions down; everyone then knows the design must change if they turn out wrong.
Say what you'll give up in advance, so nobody is surprised later.

blocks.body: If you don't turn the business goal into numbers, a design has no yardstick.

items: Ask product or the business: "What do we lose if we don't?" The answer shows how much it matters.
When you hear "properly" or "fast", ask for numbers: how many seconds, how many people, how much money.

check.q: You hear "lots of customers will come on Black Friday." What do you ask before designing?
check.a: How many? Orders per minute, for how long, and what last year's figure was. Without numbers you can't say which design is enough.

slides.title: ROI: which work comes first?
slides.tldr: Measure each project's cost and yearly gain, then see how long payback takes. Whatever earns back its cost soonest goes first.

blocks.body: To the business, every project is an investment. Before buying a new oven, a pizza place owner asks, "How many days until it pays for itself?" An engineer can ask the same. ROI (Return on Investment) = (yearly gain − cost) ÷ cost. Payback = cost ÷ monthly gain. The numbers here are examples.

blocks.code:
Project                       Cost       Yearly gain       ROI      Payback
A. Add a cache to checkout    $30,000    $60,000           +100%    6 months
   (server cost saved $20,000 + lost orders recovered $40,000)
B. New admin dashboard        $50,000    $20,000           -60%     30 months
   (saves support hours)
C. Split into services        $120,000   $90,000           -25%     16 months
   (pays off if the team grows later)

Calculation: A = (6-3)/3 = 1.0 -> 100%; payback = 3/(6/12) = 6 months (in units of $10,000)
Caution: the gain figures are estimates; risk reduction isn't counted here.

marks.tip: Write down where the gain comes from. If you don't explain how $60,000 arrives, nobody will believe it.
The ROI formula worked by hand. Anyone can check it for themselves.
Not all value can be put in dollars, such as reduced security risk. ROI is only one lens.

blocks.caption: Months until the cost is earned back (lower is better)

items.label: A. cache
items.tip: It earns back its cost fastest, so it goes first.

items.label: C. split services
items.tip: The gain depends on the future, so it is uncertain.

items.label: B. dashboard
items.tip: It doesn't earn back its cost even in a year; this one can wait.

blocks.body: ROI doesn't make the decision. It only shows how quickly each project earns back its cost.

items: Taking the ROI numbers as truth. They are estimates, so present them as a range.
Security, compliance and risk-reduction work looks small in ROI, yet the loss from skipping it is big. Treat it separately.

check.q: Which project goes first: A, which pays back in 6 months, or B at 30 months?
check.a: A, because it earns back its cost quickly. If B has a risk or legal side, that is a separate consideration, even though its gain is smaller.

slides.title: Fast or good: where to give, where not to
slides.tldr: Not every place needs the same quality. Cut corners where a mistake is cheap, but never on money, security or data.

blocks.body: On the night before Thanksgiving, a baker might leave the crust edges a little uneven, but she never gets the sugar and salt wrong. She cuts corners where the customer won't notice or where it's easy to fix. Software works the same way: when time is short, decide first where you can give.

blocks.caption: Where you can give, and where you can't

columns.title: Can give when time is short
items: Styling of the admin pages
Speed of a rarely used report
Internal code polish (log the debt)
A friendly message for a rare edge case
columns.tip: A mistake here costs little, and it is easy to fix later.

columns.title: Cannot give
items: Accuracy of money and orders
Permission checks and security
Data loss or backups
Users' personal data
columns.tip: A mistake here means losing money or trust, and it is hard to fix later.

blocks.title: What you must do when you give
items: Write down what you gave up, as a debt.
Set when you'll pay it back: a date or a sprint.
Tell the business what risk you are taking.

blocks.body: You can trade quality for speed, but a hidden debt keeps growing.

aside.title: Cutting corners on the crust
aside.body: In its rush to launch, one startup left the admin pages unfinished but wrote the payment tests in full. Two months later the admin pages were fixed, and nothing ever went wrong with payments. The corner was cut in the right place.

items: Imagine a team skipping the duplicate-charge test to launch a week sooner. One slow-network day, 300 customers are charged twice; refunds and lost trust cost more than that week.
Calling everything "cuttable". If an admin page holds the refund button, it isn't cosmetic: check what a page can do before you cut it.

check.q: Time is short. Which do you cut: the polish on the admin pages, or the payment tests?
check.a: The admin page polish. A payment bug costs both money and trust, and is hard to fix later.

slides.title: Legal rules: an input at the start of design
slides.tldr: Legal rules decide where data lives, for how long, and who may see it. Learn them at the start of design, not at the end.

blocks.body: To open a pharmacy you need a license from the drug regulator, and there are rules on where medicines may be stored. Draw the store layout first and you'll have to tear it down and rebuild. Software is the same. Picture a small loan app that keeps customer records in a cloud region abroad. A year in, the regulator says financial data must stay inside the US. Now the database, the backups and the logs all have to move while live customers keep paying, and that can take months. One question in week one would have cost an afternoon.

blocks.caption: From legal rules to design decisions: five questions

steps.title: 1. What data?
steps.body: Is there personal, financial or health data?
steps.tip: The kind of data decides which rules apply. Start by listing your data.

steps.title: 2. Where will it live?
steps.body: Must it stay in the country? Which cloud regions are allowed?
steps.tip: Some rules require data to stay inside the country. That affects your choice of cloud region.

steps.title: 3. How long do we keep it?
steps.body: How long must we keep it, and when must we delete it?
steps.tip: There are minimum retention periods, but personal data also can't be kept longer than needed.

steps.title: 4. Who can see it?
steps.body: Who has access to which data, and where is the record?
steps.tip: Limiting access and keeping an audit log are common demands of almost every set of rules.

steps.title: 5. What is the proof?
steps.body: What will you show when an auditor comes?
steps.tip: Following the rules is not enough; you have to show it. Proof is part of the design.

blocks.body: Legal rules can't be changed. So they are a constraint at the start of design, not a hassle at the end.

items: Putting the legal side off with "I'll look at it later". Moving data to a different location later is very expensive.
Interpreting the law yourself. For a specific rule, talk to compliance or a legal expert.

check.q: Why do you need to know the legal rules at the start of design?
check.a: Because if data location, retention and access aren't settled early, changing them later takes months. With the rules assumed up front, the design is right the first time.

slides.title: Worked example: the five questions for a small loan app
slides.tldr: Answer the five questions in writing before design. Each answer becomes something you can build or check: a region, a purge job, an access rule, an audit table.

blocks.body: Back to the loan app. Before any design, fill in one page. The numbers and rules below are examples; your real ones come from a compliance person or a lawyer. Notice that every answer ends in something you can build or check.

blocks.code:
App: small loan app (name, phone, photo ID, loan history)

1. What data?   Personal (name, phone, ID photo) and financial (loan history).
2. Where?       Database, backups and logs: a data center inside the US.
                (assumed rule: financial data stays in the US)
3. How long?    Loan records: keep 7 years after the loan closes (assumed).
                Rejected applicant's ID photo: delete after 90 days.
4. Who sees?    Support: name and phone only. Collections: loan history.
                ID photos: 2 named admins. Every view is logged.
5. Proof?       audit_log table (append-only) + a monthly export for the auditor.

Without this page: the region is picked by habit, photos are kept forever,
and the auditor hears "we think so".

marks.tip: The region is now a design input, chosen on day one. Backups and logs count too: a copy abroad breaks the rule as much as the database does.
A rule with a number can become a job. The next block builds this line.
Access is by role, not by default. Logging every view is what makes question 5 answerable.

blocks.code:
-- Nightly job (PostgreSQL), run by the Symfony Scheduler. Rule from question 3.
WITH purged AS (
  DELETE FROM id_documents d
  USING applications a
  WHERE d.application_id = a.id
    AND a.status = 'rejected'
    AND a.decided_at < now() - interval '90 days'
  RETURNING d.id
)
INSERT INTO audit_log (action, subject_id, at)
SELECT 'id_document_purged', id, now() FROM purged;

marks.tip: The 90 days from question 3, written once, in the one place that enforces it.
Delete and log are one statement, so a photo is never gone without a record. This row is the proof for question 5.

items: Copying the example numbers. The 7 years and 90 days here are made up; yours come from compliance.
Deleting from the live table but forgetting backups, logs and exports. The rule covers every copy.

use: The app holds personal, financial or health data
Before you pick a cloud region or a database
avoid: A throw-away prototype with fake data (redo this page before real data arrives)
Deciding what the law says; that is for compliance or a lawyer

check.q: In the loan app, which answer tells you to build a nightly purge job, and what else must the job write?
check.a: Question 3: rejected ID photos are deleted after 90 days. For each deletion the job also writes an audit_log row, which is the proof for the auditor.

slides.title: When the wedding arrangements fall apart
slides.tldr: Even with sound technology, a project runs late if the team, the plan, the time estimates, the vendors and the hiring aren't right.

blocks.body: In September, Ryan said, "The app launches in November." In November it turned out that the payment team's API wasn't built, the SMS vendor was stuck on contract terms, the new hire never arrived, and the estimate had been a single number: "6 weeks." There was nothing wrong with the code.

blocks.title: Arranging a wedding
blocks.body: A wedding has separate crews for cooking, decorating and looking after guests. If the caterer doesn't show up, everything stalls, so you talk to them well in advance. Who delivers what, and when, is written down. A software project is an event to organize too.

blocks.caption: Where projects break, and which slide in this segment fixes it

cells: The cooking crew is also decorating
rows.tip: When responsibilities and boundaries are unclear, nobody finishes anything, and everyone interferes with everyone else's work.
If another team or an outsider doesn't deliver on time, your work stalls too.

cells: "The cooking will be done in fifteen minutes"
rows.tip: A single number is a false promise; give a range and your assumptions, and trust stays intact.
A small clause in a contract can do big damage later.

cells: The wrong people, or too few
rows.tip: Fixing a bad hire is the most expensive fix of all.

blocks.body: Projects most often break outside the code: in people, time and contracts.

aside.body: A technically strong engineer can still sink under organizational weakness. This segment teaches five fundamentals of organizing work.

items.label: Conway's Law: how teams and design relate

check.q: Why did Ryan's project run late when there was nothing wrong with the code?
check.a: The other team's API, the vendor's contract and the hiring delay weren't planned for in advance, and the estimate was a single number, not a range.

slides.title: Four kinds of teams
slides.tldr: One clear job per team cuts overload and hand-offs. The four kinds: stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem. Under about 10 engineers, one team is enough.

blocks.body: Ryan's company had 16 engineers in one team that owned checkout, a pricing model and the deploy pipeline (the machinery that tests and ships code). A pricing bug waited three weeks because its one expert was busy fixing the pipeline, and checkout releases stopped whenever she was away.

blocks.caption: One team holding everything vs teams with one job each

columns.title: One team holds everything
items: Checkout, pricing model and pipeline in one team
A pricing bug waits three weeks for its one expert
Releases stop when the pipeline person is away
columns.tip: Too much for any head to hold. Every job queues behind the same few experts.

columns.title: Each team has one job
items: A checkout team that owns only the buying flow
Pricing specialists own the model; checkout just calls it
A platform team keeps the pipeline healthy for everyone
columns.tip: Each team can hold its whole area in its head, so work stops queueing behind one person.

blocks.body: A wedding avoids this: one person looks after guests, one supplies kitchen equipment, one trains newcomers, and one cook alone makes the special dish (say, the wedding cake). The book Team Topologies names the same four roles for teams.

blocks.caption: The four kinds of teams (Team Topologies)

cells: One flow of the business, start to finish
rows.tip: Most teams are this type. They create value directly for users.

cells: Tools that make others' work easier
rows.tip: It lowers the load on stream teams. Run the platform like a product, not as a mandatory rulebook.
It helps for a while, then steps away. It doesn't create a permanent dependency.
A part that takes deep expertise to understand, so it lives in its own team.

blocks.title: Rules for splitting teams, and when to skip them
items: Keep teams small (about 5 to 9 people), so everyone can talk to everyone.
Cognitive load is how much a team must keep in its head at once. When it is too much, split the team.
Team structure shapes system structure, so decide first what you want to split.
Fewer than about 10 engineers? Keep one team; four types would be paperwork. Split when work queues behind one person or nobody understands the whole.
A platform team imposes rules without listening to what its user teams need.
Creating one team per service, so nobody sees the whole picture.

check.q: One team handles checkout, complex payment rules and CI/CD all at once. What goes wrong, and what do you do?
check.a: The cognitive load is too high. Move the hard part to a complicated-subsystem team and CI/CD to a platform team, so the checkout team can focus on its own flow.

slides.title: Roadmap and dependencies
slides.tldr: Write outcomes, not features, in the roadmap (Now / Next / Later). Give every dependency an owner and a date, or the delay shows up at the end.

blocks.body: A wedding organizer keeps a list: who delivers what, and when. A project's roadmap and dependency list are the same thing. Put dates on features and you make false promises; give outcomes and time stages and you keep some flexibility.

blocks.code:
BEFORE: "Refund feature, 15 Nov"   <- a date that breaks the day the payment API slips

ROADMAP (Now / Next / Later)
Now   (this quarter, committed):  checkout p95 under 1 second
Next  (next quarter, likely):     coupons and offers
Later (afterwards, uncertain):    payments in foreign currency

DEPENDENCY REGISTER
# Dependency              Owner          We need it by   Status       Risk
1 Payment team refund API  Payment team   15 Nov          In design    High
2 SMS vendor sandbox       Vendor/Sarah    20 Nov          Contract open  Medium
3 Security review          Security team  25 Nov          Booked       Low

Rule: any dependency needed in under 2 weeks with status "In design" or behind
      gets a red flag at the weekly stand-up.

marks.tip: A feature with a date is a promise. It breaks the moment something the feature waits on slips.
Now is a firm commitment, Next is likely, Later is a wish. p95 under 1 second means 95 of every 100 checkouts finish within a second.
Each dependency has one owner and the date we need it. Nobody watches a dependency with no owner.
The needed-by date is close and the work is behind, so it gets a red flag early. Finding out at the last minute does the most damage.

blocks.caption: What our feature stands on

nodes.label: Refund feature
nodes.tip: What we want to deliver on time.

nodes.label: Payment team API
nodes.tip: Still in design. The biggest risk.

nodes.label: SMS vendor
nodes.tip: The contract is still open, and we need it to get the sandbox, a safe test copy of the vendor's service. It will take time, but it won't block the work for now.

edges.label: Without the refund API, our work can't even start
To text customers, we need the vendor's sandbox
The security review must pass before launch

blocks.body: A dependency with no owner is the one whose delay surprises you most.

items: Write outcomes, not features: not "feature X" but "cut checkout drop-off by 20%".
Spend 5 minutes a week on the dependency list. If one is red, ask the owner directly.
Putting exact feature dates on a roadmap; later, the promises break.
Hiding a date that really is fixed. If a law or a holiday sale fixes it, write that date down; Now / Next / Later is for work whose date is soft.

check.q: Why use Now / Next / Later on a roadmap instead of exact dates?
check.a: Far-off dates carry more uncertainty. Three levels keep committed, likely and uncertain work apart, and avoid false promises.

slides.title: Estimation: a range, not a single number
slides.tldr: An estimate is a range plus its assumptions, not one number. Three points per task (best, likely, worst) give the expected time and the range.

blocks.body: When someone asks, "How long will this take?", saying "6 weeks" is easy, and wrong. A single number sounds like a promise. A range (say, 15 to 21 days) with the assumptions it depends on lets everyone see the uncertainty up front. The range isn't a feeling: it comes from how far apart each task's best and worst are.

blocks.code:
Task                 best  likely  worst   expected = (best + 4×likely + worst) ÷ 6
A. OTP at login         3      5     10    (3 + 20 + 10) ÷ 6 = 5.5 days
B. Coupon model         2      3      6    (2 + 12 + 6) ÷ 6 = 3.3 days
C. Add SMS vendor       5      8     20    (5 + 32 + 20) ÷ 6 = 9.5 days
----------------------------------------------------------------
Total expected                                           ≈ 18 days

Spread of one task = (worst - best) ÷ 6:    A 1.2    B 0.7    C 2.5
Spread of the total = √(1.2² + 0.7² + 2.5²) = √8.2 ≈ 2.9 days
Range = 18 ± 2.9  ->  15 to 21 days (roughly 2 times in 3)

Announce: "About 18 days, most likely 15 to 21."
Assumptions: the vendor sandbox arrives by the 20th; nobody is dedicated to testing.
Risk: if the vendor is late, C hits its worst case: 5.5 + 3.3 + 20 ≈ 29 days.

marks.tip: Three points: the best case, the most likely, and the worst. This is called the PERT formula.
Spread is the give-or-take. The more a task's worst case sits above its best, the wider it is. C alone adds 6.25 of the 8.2 under the root.
Spreads are squared, added and rooted, not simply added: tasks rarely all go badly at once. This holds only if they fail independently.
Announce it with a range; avoid giving a single number.
With the assumptions written down, it's easy to discuss the cause if they turn out wrong.

blocks.caption: Expected days per task (best-worst in brackets)

items.label: C. SMS vendor
items.tip: The widest range, because of an outside dependency.

blocks.body: A single number turns into a promise. State the range and the assumptions, and you stay honest.

items: Treating an estimate as a deadline. An estimate is a guess; a deadline is a promise.
Quoting a lower number under pressure. The work doesn't shrink; the delay just shows up later.
Treating the range as a guarantee. It assumes tasks go wrong independently; one shared cause, like a late vendor, hits several at once, so state it as an assumption.

check.q: Why is the estimate for task C so wide, 5 to 20 days, and what do you do about it?
check.a: It depends on a vendor, which adds uncertainty. First make sure you get the vendor's sandbox, or run a small spike, to narrow the range.

slides.title: Vendors and contracts: what to check before signing
slides.tldr: If you don't read the contract, you may have no way out later. Check the SLA, data return, price rises, liability and exit terms first.

blocks.body: A contract with a caterer says how many people's food, what happens if they're late, and what compensation applies if the food is bad. A software vendor is no different. Imagine Sarah's team signs with an SMS gateway for its low first-year price. In year two the price doubles on 30 days' notice, and leaving means waiting 90 days for an export of their data. The salesperson talked nicely, but what counts is in the contract. Run through the list below before you sign.

blocks.code:
Vendor: SMS gateway X    Evaluator: Sarah    Decision date: 30 November

[ ] SLA: what is the uptime (say, 99.9%)? What compensation if they miss it?
[ ] Data return: if we leave, in what format and how fast do we get our data back?
[ ] Price: fixed for how long? How much notice before a price rise?
[ ] Exit: how many days' notice? Any minimum term or penalty?
[ ] Security: where do they keep the data? Which certifications?
[ ] Liability: if they cause a loss, what is the maximum they owe?
[ ] Alternative: is a second vendor identified? How fast could we switch?

Most important for us: data return + exit (to avoid lock-in)

marks.tip: An SLA is a promised uptime. 99.9% still allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month (99% allows over 7 hours). Without compensation, the number is worthless.
You can't switch vendors without getting your data back. This is the main trap of lock-in.
The liability cap is often tiny, such as one month's fee. Find out.
With no alternative, you have no bargaining power.

blocks.caption: Five steps to choosing a vendor

steps.title: 1. Write the need
steps.body: What problem to solve, which numbers matter?
steps.tip: If you don't write down your needs, the salesperson decides what you want.

steps.title: 2. Compare two or three
steps.body: Build a matrix and score the options.
steps.tip: Talk to only one and you have no room to negotiate.

steps.title: 3. Ask for proof
steps.body: A sandbox, reference customers, an uptime record.
steps.tip: Don't take their word. Test it yourself.

steps.title: 4. Read the contract
steps.body: Check the risk terms with the legal team.
steps.tip: It's the small print that divides responsibility. Get legal advice.

steps.title: 5. Plan the exit
steps.body: Write down in advance how long it would take to switch.
steps.tip: Before you sign, know how you would leave.

items: Treating a salesperson's promise as the contract. If it's not in the contract, it's nothing.
Signing for the low first-year price without reading the price-rise terms.

use: The vendor holds your data or sits on a critical path, such as payments or SMS login codes
The contract has a minimum term or a long notice period
avoid: A low-spend tool billed monthly that you could swap in a day: read the price and exit terms only

check.q: To keep a way out of a vendor, which two terms do you check most closely before signing?
check.a: Data return (what format, how fast) and the exit terms (notice, penalty). Without those two, you get caught in the vendor's net.

slides.title: Hiring: a scorecard, not a gut feeling
slides.tldr: Ask every candidate the same questions, score them on the same criteria, with evidence. Otherwise "I liked them" becomes the decision.

blocks.body: Two candidates at an interview. One talks the way we do, and we liked them. The other gives less polished answers but is stronger at code. Choose by "liked them" and the first wins. With a scorecard, you compare by scoring against criteria fixed in advance.

blocks.code:
Role: Backend Engineer    Candidate: A    Interviewer: Sarah    Date: 10 December

Skill                           Weight  Score (1-4)  Evidence (what they said/did)
Design (understands trade-offs)    3        3        "separated the cost of queue and cache"
Code and debugging                 3        4        "spotted N+1 on their own, and fixed it"
Communication                      2        2        "started without asking, assuming"
Eagerness to learn                 2        3        "admitted a mistake, had read up"

Total: 3×3 + 3×4 + 2×2 + 2×3 = 9 + 12 + 4 + 6 = 31 / 40
Recommendation: Hire / No hire / Another round    Reason: ........
Rule: each person writes their score first, then we discuss.

marks.tip: The criteria and weights are fixed before the interview; they aren't changed after seeing a candidate.
Without the evidence column, a score is just an opinion. Write what the candidate said or did.
The arithmetic: 9 + 12 + 4 + 6 = 31, out of a maximum of 40.
If everyone writes their score before the discussion, one person's view doesn't sway the rest.

blocks.caption: A chat-style interview vs a structured interview

columns.title: A casual chat
items: Different questions each time
The decision is "I liked them"
More points for people like me
columns.tip: Each candidate gets a different experience, so comparing is hard, and bias creeps in.

columns.title: Structured
items: The same questions for everyone
Criteria and weights set in advance
Scores with evidence, written separately
columns.tip: The same questions and the same yardstick. Less bias, a fairer comparison.

blocks.body: Hiring is one of the costliest decisions: criteria first, gut feeling after.

items: Picking people like yourself in the name of culture fit. A mix of skills is also a team's strength.
Asking only trivia or algorithm puzzles, with no link to real work situations.
Treating the total as the verdict. A weighted total can hide a fatal gap: set a minimum for the must-have skills before you add up.
Ask questions from real work: "Fix this slow query" or "What are the risks in this design?"
Write up your scores as soon as possible after the interview, before memory fades.

check.q: Why does a scorecard have an "evidence" column?
check.a: Without evidence, a score is only an opinion. Writing what the candidate said or did makes the comparison fair and exposes bias.

slides.title: Everyone's going, so should we?
slides.tldr: New technology is exciting, but shouldering a solution built for someone else's problem can freeze features for six months.

blocks.body: On a team of 5, Jake said, "The big companies use microservices and Kubernetes, so let's do it too." Six months went into infrastructure. In that time not a single new feature shipped, and the app had 2,000 users. The problem wasn't the technology. Nobody had asked, "Which problem of ours is this for?"

blocks.title: This year's trendy sneakers
blocks.body: The sneakers everyone is buying on Black Friday may not fit you. They cost more, are bulky, and every store sells the same pair. Know your own size first, then look at the trend.

blocks.caption: Two teams, six months later

columns.title: Chasing the hype
items: 6 months on infrastructure
Zero new features
Extra people needed to manage the complexity
columns.tip: Buying the solution before knowing the problem.

columns.title: Problem first
items: One monolith, running well
Six features shipped
Will split it when a real need appears
columns.tip: Measured its own problem first. 2,000 users means a handful of requests a second, which one ordinary server handles easily.

blocks.body: Just because someone else uses it doesn't mean you need it. Measure your own problem first.

items.meaning: One app split into many small apps that talk to each other over the network.
A system for running and managing many containers across many servers.
The whole app as one piece, deployed together.

aside.body: This segment teaches you to stay skeptical while learning something new, to put reality ahead of rules, and to own the long-term consequences of your decisions.

check.q: Why did Jake's team lose six months?
check.a: They never measured their own problem. A big company's solution was extra complexity for their small problem, and nobody asked "Which problem of ours is this for?"

slides.title: Learn the new thing, but ask questions
slides.tldr: When you see a new technology, ask five questions: what problem, what alternatives, what cost, has anyone run it for years, and can we go back?

blocks.body: You shouldn't stop learning, and you shouldn't jump at everything either. When a new medicine reaches pharmacies, the pharmacist asks: for whom, what trials were done, what are the side effects? Technology needs the same skepticism. Fit the five questions below into a short evaluation template.

blocks.code:
Technology: ...........   Evaluator: ........   Date: ........

1. What problem does it solve?
   Do we have that problem? Evidence (numbers): ........
2. What are the alternatives? Why isn't the current way working?
3. Cost: learning + running + replacing. How many person-months?
4. Proof: has someone our size run it in production for 2+ years?
   (a user's experience, not the vendor's blog)
5. Can we go back? What would going back cost?

Trial: a one-week spike, on one small, low-risk piece of work.
Decision: Adopt / Run a trial / Look again later / No     Reason: ........

marks.tip: If there is no problem, the solution is pointless. Show in numbers how big our problem is.
Learning takes time, running takes people, and replacing takes time again. Count all three.
A new technology's problems appear after years in production. That is why other people's experience is valuable.
Start with a limited trial (a spike); if it works, grow it slowly.

blocks.caption: Four steps to adopting new technology

steps.title: 1. Measure the problem
steps.body: Which problem of ours, and how big, in numbers.
steps.tip: If you have no problem, there is no need to buy the solution.

steps.title: 2. Ask the questions
steps.body: Write down the answers to the five questions.
steps.tip: A lot of hype gets caught just by writing the answers.

steps.title: 3. A small spike
steps.body: One week, on low-risk work.
steps.tip: Gather some small experience before a big decision.

steps.title: 4. Decide and record
steps.body: Adopt or reject, and write the reason.
steps.tip: If someone asks next year, you have an answer.

blocks.body: Problem first, then solution. Do it the other way around and the solution becomes the problem.

items.meaning: A short, throwaway experiment whose only job is to teach you something.

items: Treating a vendor's conference talk as neutral evidence.
Resume-driven development: choosing technology for your own CV.

check.q: When evaluating new technology, what is the very first question, and why?
check.a: "Which problem of ours is this for, and how big is it?" Without a problem, however good the solution, it is just extra cost.

slides.title: The five questions, filled in for Jake
slides.tldr: Run the microservices idea through the template: with real numbers, the answer is a written "no" plus the sign that would reopen it.

blocks.body: Here is Jake's idea run through the template. It takes an afternoon, and the numbers are examples; measure your own. Five requests a second is five people walking through one store door every second: one clerk copes. A "no" today isn't forever, so the last line says what would reopen the question. For a library you can swap in a day, five lines of notes are enough.

blocks.code:
Technology: microservices + Kubernetes   Evaluator: Jake   Date: 3 March

1. Problem: do we have a scale problem? Evidence: 2,000 users, about 5 requests a
   second at peak, and the server runs at 15% CPU. No.
2. Alternatives: keep the monolith (one app, one deploy). If it ever strains, a
   second server behind a load balancer.
3. Cost: 3 people x 6 months to learn and set up, then one person on call for good.
4. Proof: every company we found has hundreds of engineers. None our size.
5. Going back: merging many services into one app again takes months.

Trial: not needed.   Decision: No.
Reason: no measured problem, high cost, hard to undo.
Revisit if: peak passes 200 requests a second, or 3 teams block each other's deploys.

marks.tip: Users, requests a second and CPU are numbers anyone can check. They show we have no scale problem.
The cost is counted in people and months, so six months of infrastructure is visible before it is spent.
The trigger is a number someone can watch, so the "no" can turn into a "yes" without a new argument.

blocks.body: A written "no" with a trigger costs an afternoon. A wrong "yes" costs six months.

items.meaning: A front door that spreads incoming requests across several servers.
The whole app as one piece, deployed together.

items: Put the revisit trigger where someone will see it, such as a dashboard number, not only in a document.

check.q: Besides "no", what do the last lines of the filled-in template give the team?
check.a: The reason (no measured problem) and a trigger that reopens the question, such as peak load passing a number.

slides.title: What to learn so it still pays off in 10 years
slides.tldr: Tools change every few years; fundamental ideas don't. Put most of your learning time into fundamentals and a little into tools.

blocks.body: Accountants of the old days kept their books with pen and paper ledgers; now everyone uses a spreadsheet. The tool changed, but the debit-and-credit rules are the same. Technology works that way too. You have to learn a new version of a framework again and again, but learn the ideas of transactions, caching or consistency and they serve you for years.

blocks.caption: Tools vs fundamentals: where to invest your learning

columns.title: Tools (change fast)
items: A new framework version
A new ORM or library
One cloud's console
columns.tip: Useful, but out of date within a few years. Learn them as needed.

columns.title: Fundamentals (long-lasting)
items: Data modeling and transactions
Concurrency and failure
Networks, caching, security
Trade-offs and communication
columns.tip: These help in any tool. The biggest long-term investment.

blocks.title: A weekly learning habit
items: Spend 2 hours a week on fundamentals: read a book chapter or an article, then write it up in your own words.
Do one small project or spike a month, and run what you've learned by hand.
Learn a tool when work needs it (just in time), and don't worry about the rest.

blocks.body: Tools are rented clothes; fundamentals are your own body. Build the body first.

items: Explain what you've learned to someone else, or give a short talk to the team; your understanding gets deeper.
An idea that survives year after year is fundamental; if it changes in three years, it's a tool.

aside.body: Principles last 10 years, tools last 3. Split your learning time in the same proportion.

check.q: You have 2 hours a week to learn. Which gets more: a new framework version, or the idea of transactions?
check.a: The idea of transactions. It helps in any tool, and a framework's new version can be learned when work needs it.

slides.title: Understand the purpose before you break the rule
slides.tldr: Behind every rule there is a problem. If your project doesn't have that problem, a simpler path beats following the rule.

blocks.body: Cook for four people at home by a big catering kitchen's rules and the cooking never finishes. Rules have a purpose. If the purpose doesn't apply to you, the rule is just extra weight. Keep complexity proportionate: only as much solution as there is problem.

blocks.caption: What a rule is for, and when the simple way is fine

cells: An interface and repository for everything
Easy to swap the data source
The source is never going to change
rows.tip: If there's no chance of change, the extra layer only makes the code harder to read.

cells: Not for a plain admin CRUD; always for money
rows.tip: What matters is not the percentage but whether the risky behavior is tested.

cells: A small team with little traffic: a monolith
rows.tip: Split when you have more teams or need a different scale, not before.
Denormalization with a written reason is fine; done without knowing why, it is debt.

marks.tip: The "by the book" version: four files to read and keep in sync, for a list of 20 rows.
The written reason and the trigger are what turn a shortcut into a decision.

blocks.body: Follow a rule by understanding its purpose. Without the purpose, take the simple path, and write down why.

items: Not writing down why you broke a rule; later, nobody will know it was deliberate.
Building something complex now because "we might need it later" (YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It).

use: The problem is real and provable right now
A mistake is costly: money, security, data
avoid: Adding an extra layer only because "it could happen in the future"
Accepting someone else's made-up rule without understanding it

check.q: In a small admin CRUD, is it good to build an interface and a repository for every class?
check.a: Usually not. If the source is unlikely to change, the extra layer just adds complexity. Add it when the problem becomes real.

slides.title: Your decision is still running three years later
slides.tldr: Responsibility for a decision doesn't end when you make it. Measure the outcome, look back at a set time, and don't let debt pile up.

blocks.body: Anyone who builds a house knows a design mistake turns into a crack a few years later. In software too, today's decision lands later, often on someone else's shoulders. Owning it means measuring the result, looking back after six months, and speaking up yourself when you got it wrong.

blocks.code:
Decision: notifications as a module inside the main app (RFC-0012)
Owner: Ryan          Date: 12 December         Review: 12 June

We assumed:        fewer than 2,000 messages a day; a team of 4
What we'll measure: messages a day; queue delay (p95 = the slowest 1 in 20);
                    how often this module broke
Questions for the review:
  - Was the assumption right? (How many messages now?)
  - What turned out harder than we thought?
  - Would we make the same decision today?
Result: ........   Next step: keep / change / repay (debt)

marks.tip: One owner and a review date fixed in advance. Otherwise "we'll look later" never happens.
With the assumptions written down, you can check them later, and learn if they were wrong.
The numbers are agreed already, so the review looks at facts, not opinions.
The last question is the most honest: knowing what we know, would we make the same decision today?

blocks.caption: Five steps to owning a decision

steps.title: 1. Write it down
steps.body: The decision, the reason, the assumptions: in an ADR or RFC.
steps.tip: If it isn't written, the reason is lost after six months.

steps.title: 2. Pick an owner
steps.body: One person, by name.
steps.tip: Everyone's responsibility means no one's.

steps.title: 3. Choose the measures
steps.body: Which number tells us it's going well?
steps.tip: If the measures aren't fixed first, you can pick numbers you like later.

steps.title: 4. Look back
steps.body: A review after six months or a year.
steps.tip: Put it in the calendar; forgetting is the most natural thing.

steps.title: 5. Repay the debt
steps.body: If there are mistakes or accumulated debt, list them and make time.
steps.tip: If there's a gap between saying and repaying, trust falls.

blocks.body: Whoever makes the decision owns the outcome. Don't leave it assuming someone else will handle it.

aside.title: The six-month review
aside.body: A team looked back at its queue decision after six months. They had assumed 2,000 messages a day; the real number was 20,000. The queue delay (p95) had grown from 2 seconds to 40. Because the review was already in the calendar, they saw it before customers complained, moved to another transport in two weeks, and no major incident followed.

items.meaning: Architecture Decision Record: a short note of one decision, its reason and its consequences.
Shortcuts and old choices you will have to pay back later with extra work.

check.q: Why are the measures agreed in advance, together with the decision?
check.a: When they're fixed first, the review looks at facts, not opinions. Otherwise there is a tendency to pick the numbers you like.
